correctness.rationale: The cited generating function is for the tagged total in odd-part designated-summand partitions, not the partition count or the unrestricted tagged total. Factoring its eta quotient as qE(q²⁴)P(q)/[P(q³)P(q¹²)] is exact. The product for P has constant term 1 and nonconstant terms in each factor of the form 2q^(mj); modulo four only one factor can contribute, giving twice the divisor count, which is odd precisely on squares. The shifted inverses negate those terms; Euler's pentagonal identity yields qE(q²⁴)=Σ_t(−1)^tq^((6t−1)²). The signs on pentagonal terms survive only for epsilon, since 2 and −2 coincide modulo four in the representation terms. For n≡3 modulo 4 none of the square or representation terms can contribute. For primes p≡1 modulo 4 the j in the d=3 term is even, making its count identical to the d=12 count, and their contributions cancel. For p≥5 the unique odd coordinate in the prime two-square representation contributes exactly once iff 3 does not divide it: one sign then lies in the class −1 modulo 6. The examples and small prime exclusions agree. For r≡11 modulo 12, both −1 and −3 are nonsquares, so r-divisibility of either relevant norm form forces both variables divisible by r, implying even r-valuation by descent; the square term also has even valuation. The lower relative prime density bound 1/4 follows from the prime number theorem in arithmetic progressions for p≡5 modulo 12 (ordinary Dirichlet infinitude alone is not a quantitative density proof). If infinitude of both subclasses of p≡1 modulo 12 is intended, it follows from the infinitude of primes represented by the primitive forms x²+36y² and 4x²+9y² respectively; the main residue proof does not require that result. A separately written finite expansion matched all 2000 positive coefficients, 301 primes from 5 to 2000 and 565 odd-valuation obstruction cases, as well as all 500 indices congruent to 3 modulo 4; see /workspace/branches/ca952bde-a00e-4cbc-aa60-263aec4fa262/check-notes.md. The supplied checker was inspected, not run; the finite replay does not prove the infinite statements.

evidence: Barman et al. prove density-one vanishing modulo powers of 2 and 3 and vanishing modulo 2^u on products of sufficiently many distinct primes coprime to 6. Their Theorem 1.4 includes a threshold s+u and is not a criterion for an individual inert prime with odd exponent. Li–Tang studies powers of 3 rather than this 2-primary residue.
broader_coverage.reasoning: These theorems are stronger for lacunarity and certain multiprime congruences. Neither gives both residue possibilities at primes, and neither selects the odd Gaussian coordinate or supplies the single-inert-prime composite rule.

evidence: The earlier product determines every coefficient, and indeed is the starting point here. Converting it into the explicit signed single-square plus three norm counts uses the overpartition-factor reduction and oddness of divisor counts on squares. The prime rule further uses an exact cancellation between the 3 and 12 forms and the sign restriction on the odd Gaussian coordinate. The reviewed modular forms in Barman et al. use an auxiliary eta quotient for lacunarity, not that classification.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: This is a short derivation from a known generating function, not a new generating function. It provides an arithmetic law not furnished by the prior progression, lacunarity or multiprime theorems and not obtained merely by enumerating coefficients.

value.rationale: The quadratic reduction turns the known coefficient generator into an all-index arithmetic test. It both distinguishes the two residues at split primes using a natural Gaussian-coordinate invariant and gives a local vanishing criterion at composite indices; density-one lacunarity or a list of residue progressions does not answer those questions. The characterization is useful even without exact densities for both Gaussian-coordinate subclasses.
